summary: Defines a MIB for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 networks. It was replaced by RFC 4087.

eli5.summary: A control panel listing the tunnels that carry traffic across the Internet and their settings.

questions: how do you manage tunnels with snmp
subtitle: Management interface for monitoring and controlling IP tunnels.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to monitor and manage IP tunnels of different types (GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TP, etc.) across their network using SNMP management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) that lists tunnel endpoints, encapsulation methods, security settings, and other parameters. It provides two tables: one for viewing configured tunnels and another for creating or deleting tunnels dynamically.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can query and manage all types of IP tunnels through a unified SNMP interface. The RFC was replaced by RFC 4087.

sections.title: Why Manage Tunnels
sections.content:
IP tunnels are virtual connections that encapsulate one type of traffic inside another IP packet. Common uses include GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation), IP-in-IP, L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol), PPTP (Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol), Minimal Encapsulation, and tunneling of IPv6 traffic over IPv4 networks. Each has different protocol requirements and configuration options.

Managing these tunnels manually is impractical in large networks. Network operators need a standard way to query which tunnels exist on each router, check their configuration, monitor their status, and create or delete them as needed. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and Management Information Bases (MIBs) provide this capability. This MIB defines a common interface for managing any type of IP tunnel over IPv4 networks.
sections.eli5: You have many different kinds of secret passages (tunnels) in your network, and you need one control panel to see them all and manage them.

sections.title: The Two-Table Model
sections.content:
The MIB contains two main tables. The Tunnel Interface Table shows all tunnels currently known to a router. Each entry includes the tunnel's local endpoint address (the source IP), remote endpoint address (the destination IP), encapsulation method (GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TP, etc.), the TTL (time to live) to use in the outer header, the security method (if any, such as IPsec), and the Type of Service (ToS) settings.

The Tunnel Configuration Table is indexed by tunnel endpoints and encapsulation protocol, allowing managers to look up which interface corresponds to a given tunnel configuration, and to create or delete tunnels dynamically. This second table exists because interface indexes are assigned by the router and may change across restarts, making them unsuitable as the primary index for row creation. By using endpoint addresses as the index, managers have stable control over tunnel creation without needing to know the router's internal interface numbering.
sections.eli5: One table shows all tunnels that exist. Another table lets you create or find tunnels by their endpoints and what kind of tunnel it is.

sections.title: Tunnel Configuration Objects
sections.content:
Each tunnel in the Tunnel Interface Table has several configuration parameters. The local address is the source IP in the outer tunnel header (or 0.0.0.0 if unknown). The remote address is the destination IP. The encapsulation method specifies the type: direct (plain IP-in-IP), GRE, minimal encapsulation, L2TP, PPTP, L2F, UDP-based, or ATMP.

The hop limit (also called TTL) can be set explicitly or copied from the payload packet's header (value zero). The security method indicates whether IPsec is used between endpoints, or if security is handled by other means. The Type of Service (ToS) field controls how the outer header is marked for Quality of Service, with a special value (-2) meaning to copy it from the payload.
sections.eli5: For each tunnel, you record where it starts, where it ends, what kind of encapsulation it uses, and settings like how long packets can live and whether they are encrypted.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
This MIB works with the Interfaces MIB, which defines all network interfaces on a device. Each tunnel is represented as a logical interface with type 131 (tunnel) in the Interfaces MIB. The Tunnel MIB supplements this by providing tunnel-specific configuration details.

Extension MIBs can be created for protocol-specific parameters (e.g., GRE-specific options) or security-specific parameters (e.g., IPsec key management). This MIB intentionally focuses on parameters that apply to any type of tunnel over IPv4 and omits IPv6 tunnel management, which may be covered by separate MIBs. The layering model allows multiple tunnel types to coexist on a single interface, with each tunnel stacked via the ifStack table.
sections.eli5: This MIB hooks into the master list of all network interfaces and works with other specialized MIBs for details about specific tunnel types or security.
